posts.title: 6 months ago, I couldn't write a single line of code.
posts.body:
Today, I've built 26 working software tools.

The difference wasn't learning to code. It was learning to collaborate with AI.

Here's what nobody tells non-technical founders:

You don't need to become a developer.
You need to become a great communicator.

I'm not writing Python or JavaScript. I'm writing clear instructions.

My process:
1. I describe what I want in plain English
2. Claude Code builds it
3. I test it (does it do what I asked?)
4. I share the error if it breaks
5. We iterate until it works

The tools I've built in the last 6 months:

- A Personal Operating System that prioritizes my projects automatically
- Job listing scrapers that categorize 50K+ listings with AI
- Content systems that turn project updates into posts
- Vendor quote automation that finds contacts in 5 minutes vs 2 hours
- Financial analysis dashboards (analyzed 6 years of nonprofit data in one afternoon)

My competitive advantage isn't technical skill.

It's knowing exactly what I need and being able to articulate it clearly.

Takeaway: The best 'code' I write is plain English. If you can explain a problem clearly to a human, you can explain it to AI.
posts.cta: What would you build if coding wasn't the barrier? Drop your idea below.

posts.title: I built a Personal Operating System that runs my entire life.
tweets:
I built a Personal Operating System that runs my entire life.

Projects. Content. Finance. Family.

All managed by AI I created with zero coding experience.

Here's exactly how it works:

The problem I was solving:

Ideas scattered across 5 apps. Nothing connected. Projects started but never finished.

I needed ONE system that captures everything and tells me what to work on.

Component 1: Smart Capture

I text a Telegram bot with any idea. It auto-categorizes and adds to my backlog.

Example: 'Build a job scraper' becomes a Development project instantly.

How to build: Create a Telegram bot, connect to a database, add AI categorization.

Every idea gets scored 1-10 on:
- Productivity impact
- Learning opportunity
- Career value
- Enjoyment

Formula: (Prod x 0.3) + (Learn x 0.25) + (Career x 0.25) + (Fun x 0.2)

High scorers bubble up automatically.

Component 3: Project Activation

When I pick an idea, the system:
- Creates a project folder
- Generates a CLAUDE.md context file
- Assigns a localhost port (no conflicts!)

I'm ready to build in under 2 minutes.

Component 4: Content Engine

Every project update gets logged.

AI applies 97 viral hook formulas to turn updates into posts.

One update = 5 content pieces across platforms.

The results after 6 months:

- 26 tools built
- Zero ideas lost
- Content creation 10x faster
- Always working on highest-impact projects

How to start your own Personal OS:

1. Pick ONE area (projects OR content OR finance)
2. Document your current messy workflow
3. Ask Claude: 'Help me build a system that [captures/prioritizes/tracks] my [thing]'
4. Start with the simplest version that works

AI doesn't replace your thinking. It amplifies your execution.

You still decide what matters. AI just helps you do it faster.

Start small. One system. One problem. Build from there.

posts.title: How I generate a week of social content in 10 minutes
posts.body:
I used to spend 10+ hours every week brainstorming content.

Now my AI system does it in minutes.

The secret: I stopped asking AI to 'be creative.'

Instead, I feed it proven frameworks.

Here's the exact system:

1. Capture my actual work
Every project update, lesson learned, and breakthrough gets logged automatically. I text my Telegram bot or add a note.

2. Match to viral patterns
My system knows 97+ hook formulas:
- Contrarian: 'Why X is actually wrong'
- Transformation: 'Before vs After'
- How-to: 'The exact process for X'
- Benefit: 'How I achieved X result'

3. Generate variations
One project update becomes 5+ content pieces:
- Short X post
- LinkedIn story post
- Detailed thread
- Newsletter section

4. Apply my voice
I documented my writing patterns: dashes for emphasis, sentences starting with 'So', phrases like 'What's not to love.'

The AI doesn't sound like AI. It sounds like me.

Results after 30 days:
- 47 hooks generated
- 10 hrs/week saved
- Higher engagement (proven patterns work)

Takeaway: Content frameworks are just structured prompts. Feed AI the framework. Let it apply your context. Scale your voice without losing authenticity.

posts.title: Why your AI prompts are failing (and it's not what you think)
posts.body:
Most people write prompts like this:

'Write me a viral tweet.'

Then they're disappointed when AI outputs generic garbage.

Here's what I learned after 6 months of building with Claude Code:

AI doesn't need creativity. It needs frameworks.

Bad prompt: 'Help me brainstorm content ideas.'

Good prompt: 'Apply the Contrarian Hook formula to my project update. The formula: Challenge common assumption + reveal better approach. My update: I built a job scraper that processes 1000 listings in seconds.'

The difference:
- Bad prompt: Infinite possibilities, average output
- Good prompt: Specific framework, excellent output

I built a library of 97+ hook patterns.

Now I don't ask AI to 'be creative.'

I ask it to apply proven patterns to my specific context.

How to do this yourself:
1. Find 10 posts in your niche that performed well
2. Identify the structure (hook type, format, CTA)
3. Turn that structure into a template
4. Ask AI to apply that template to YOUR content

Takeaway: The frameworks do the creative heavy lifting. AI does the application. You do the editing. Build a library of frameworks you can combine and reuse.

How I automated vendor quote collection (saving 15+ hours/month)

The problem: Manually Googling vendors, copying contact info, sending personalized emails.

The solution: An AI system that does it all.

Here's exactly how I built it:

The old workflow (painful):

1. Google '[service] near [location]'
2. Click through 20+ results
3. Copy business name, phone, email
4. Paste into spreadsheet
5. Write personalized outreach
6. Track responses manually

10-15 hours/month. Brutal.

What I built:

Vendor Quote Collection Tool

Input: Category, location, radius
Output: Full contact database + personalized outreach drafts

The architecture is simpler than you'd think.

Component 1: Multi-platform search

Scrapes Google Maps, Yelp, and industry directories.

How: Ask Claude to build a scraper for each source. Combine results. Deduplicate by business name.

Component 2: Contact extraction

Pulls email, phone, website, hours from each listing.

How: For each result, visit the website and extract contact info. Store in a simple database.

Component 3: AI personalization

Each vendor gets a custom message based on:
- Their specific services (from their website)
- Their reviews (what customers say)
- Their location

Not mail merge. Actual personalization.

The results:

- 50+ vendor contacts in 5 minutes (vs 2 hours)
- Personalized outreach at scale
- Response rate 3x higher than templates
- 15+ hours/month saved

How to build your own:

1. Start with ONE platform (Google Maps is easiest)
2. Build a simple scraper that extracts business info
3. Add AI to write personalized messages
4. Test with 10 vendors manually first
5. Automate once you know what works

Takeaway: Automation isn't about replacing humans.

It's about removing the tedious parts so you can focus on the relationship parts.

I still have the conversations. I just don't waste time finding people to talk to.

posts.title: The exact process I use to build tools with Claude Code (as a non-developer)
posts.body:
People ask how I build software without a technical background.

Here's my exact process:

Step 1: Define the Problem Clearly

Not 'I want a scraper.'

Instead: 'I need to collect business contact info from Google search results within a 25-mile radius, extract email/phone/hours, and export to a spreadsheet.'

Specificity matters. Include: Input format, output format, any rules or constraints.

Step 2: Start with the Simplest Version

I always ask: 'What's the minimal version that would be useful?'

For my job classifier:
- V1: Upload CSV, get categorized output (command line)
- V2: Add a simple web interface
- V3: Add AI-enhanced categories with confidence scores

Ship V1 first. Always.

Step 3: Describe, Don't Dictate

I describe WHAT I need, not HOW to build it.

Bad: 'Use Python with BeautifulSoup and pandas to...'
Good: 'I need to extract contact info from business websites'

Let Claude choose the implementation.

Step 4: Test Immediately

I run the code right away. Don't try to understand it first.

Errors aren't failures - they're feedback.

I copy the exact error message and share it with Claude. It fixes. We iterate.

Step 5: Document What Works

Every successful pattern goes into my CLAUDE.md file.

This is context that persists across sessions. Claude learns my preferences over time.

Takeaway: You're not a coder. You're a product manager with an infinitely patient engineering team. Your job is clarity. Claude's job is implementation.

posts.title: I analyzed 6 years of nonprofit financial data in one afternoon.
posts.body:
A client asked me to review their organization's financial health.

6 years of IRS Form 990 data. Traditionally: Weeks of spreadsheet work.

With Claude Code: One afternoon.

Here's exactly what I did:

Step 1: Upload and extract
I uploaded the raw 990 filings and asked Claude to extract key metrics: revenue, expenses, contributions, salaries, assets.

Step 2: Calculate trends
I asked for year-over-year changes and identified which numbers were accelerating or decelerating.

Step 3: Find red flags
I asked Claude to flag concerning patterns based on nonprofit financial best practices.

Step 4: Generate summary
I asked for an executive summary with specific recommendations.

What the analysis revealed:

The organization went from consistent profitability to a $713K loss in just two years.

Root causes:
- Expenses grew 15.8% while revenue grew 8.2%
- Contributions collapsed 69.8% (from $1.3M to $399K)
- Salary costs up 35.9% over 6 years

The deliverable: A professional executive summary with specific interventions and 3-year projections.

Total time: 4 hours.

Takeaway: AI didn't do the analysis. I defined what questions to ask, validated the logic, and crafted recommendations. AI handled data processing. That's the collaboration: Human judgment + AI processing = faster, deeper analysis.

posts.title: The CLAUDE.md file changed everything about how I work with AI.
tweets:
The CLAUDE.md file changed everything about how I work with AI.

It's a context file that persists across sessions.

Claude reads it before every conversation.

Here's exactly how to use it:

The problem it solves:

Every new chat starts from zero. You re-explain your project, your preferences, your goals.

What goes in my CLAUDE.md:

1. Project overview (what I'm building, why)
2. Tech stack decisions (and reasoning)

4. What's already been built

Purpose: Job listing scraper with AI classification
Phase: Development

# Tech Stack
Backend: Python/FastAPI

'We tried approach X but it didn't work because Y.'

Claude won't suggest the same mistake twice. This is huge.

I have CLAUDE.md files in every project:

How to start:

1. Create CLAUDE.md in your project folder
2. Add: What you're building, why, how far along

The results:

- No more re-explaining context (saves 10+ min per session)
- Consistent outputs across sessions
- Claude learns my preferences over time
- Faster iteration cycles

Takeaway: CLAUDE.md is your project's memory.

Start simple. Add to it every session. Watch Claude get smarter about YOUR project.

posts.title: How I turned messy job listing data into actionable intelligence
posts.body:
A client had 50,000 job postings.

All text dumps. No structure. No categories.

They needed to understand: What jobs are actually being posted?

The challenge: Job titles are a mess.
- 'Aircraft Maintenance Technician Needed ASAP!!!'
- 'Blair Stone Location - NOW HIRING'
- 'HVAC Tech - Great Benefits - Apply Today'

Traditional approach: Manual categorization. Weeks of work.

My approach: AI classification with guardrails.

The System I Built:

1. Upload any CSV with job text

2. AI extracts the actual job title (filtering out location names, marketing fluff)

3. Classifies into specific categories:
- 'Aircraft' -> Aviation Mechanic (not generic 'Technician')
- 'Security guard jobs at airport' -> Security Guard (not 'Airport Staff')
- 'Blair Stone hiring construction' -> Construction Worker (not 'Blair Stone')

4. Confidence scoring so you know which need manual review

How to build this yourself:

1. Start with 100 rows manually categorized
2. Write rules: 'If title contains X, category is Y'
3. Give Claude your rules and examples
4. Ask it to classify the rest
5. Review low-confidence results manually

Results:
- 50,000 listings processed in hours (not weeks)
- 89% accuracy on first pass
- Specific categories that actually mean something

Takeaway: AI + clear rules beats AI + 'figure it out.' The system works because I gave it specific category definitions, examples of edge cases, and rules for what to filter out. Constraints make AI smarter.

posts.title: The voice training method that makes AI sound like you (not like AI)
posts.body:
I spent weeks trying to get AI to match my writing style.

'Write casually!'
'Be conversational!'
'Sound human!'

The outputs were garbage. Generic. Bland.

Then I tried something different.

Instead of describing my voice, I documented it.

My Voice Documentation System:

1. Vocabulary Analysis
I listed my actual word choices:
- Colloquialisms: 'thick skinned,' 'talk a good game,' 'old gal'
- Distinctive phrases: 'burns from zero to one,' 'ahead of their skis'
- Repetition patterns: I emphasize by repeating key terms

2. Grammatical Patterns
- I start sentences with 'So' and 'And'
- I use dashes liberally - like this - for emphasis
- Sentence fragments are fine. For impact.
- Active voice always

3. Punctuation Style
- Dashes for parenthetical emphasis
- Ellipses to trail off...
- Exclamation points sparingly (but not never!)

4. Content Examples
I included 10+ examples of my actual writing, annotated:
- 'This opening uses the curiosity hook'
- 'This paragraph demonstrates my teaching style'
- 'Notice how I admit uncertainty here'

How to build your own voice document:

1. Collect your 20 best posts/emails/writing samples
2. Note patterns: word choices, sentence structures, punctuation
3. Include specific examples, not just descriptions
4. Reference this document in every content prompt

Takeaway: 'Sound conversational' is useless. 'Use dashes for emphasis, start sentences with conjunctions, include self-deprecating humor' is useful. Specificity wins.

posts.title: The web scraping architecture that handles any website
posts.body:
Not all websites are created equal.

Some serve clean HTML. Some hide behind JavaScript. Some actively fight scrapers.

I built a system that handles all of them.

The Architecture: Intelligent Scraper Selection

Tier 1: Simple HTTP
For static websites with clean HTML.
- Fastest option
- Lowest resource usage
- Works for ~40% of sites

Tier 2: Headless Browser
For JavaScript-rendered content.
- Playwright automation
- Handles dynamic loading
- Works for ~50% of sites

Tier 3: Anti-Bot Bypass
For sites with sophisticated protection.
- Rotating proxies
- Browser fingerprint management
- Works for the remaining ~10%

The Smart Selection Logic:

The system automatically:
1. Tries Tier 1 first (fastest)
2. Detects JavaScript requirements
3. Identifies anti-bot measures
4. Escalates to appropriate tier
5. Falls back gracefully on failure

How to build this yourself:

1. Start with simple HTTP requests (Python requests library)
2. When that fails, add Playwright for JS sites
3. Keep a list of which approach works for which sites
4. Let Claude help you detect when to use which tier

Key Rules I Follow:
- Always respect robots.txt
- Implement rate limiting
- Rotate user agents
- Never scrape private data
- Handle errors gracefully

Takeaway: Build for the 80% case first (simple HTTP), then add complexity only where needed. Most sites don't need fancy solutions.

New things I could build. Should build. Want to build.

But which ones actually matter?

The old approach:

Pick whatever felt exciting in the moment.

Result: Lots of started projects. Few finished ones.

The new approach: Impact-based scoring.

Every idea gets rated on 4 dimensions:

1. Productivity (1-10): Will this save me time?
2. Learning (1-10): Will I gain new skills?
3. Career (1-10): Will this advance my goals?
4. Enjoyment (1-10): Will I actually want to work on this?

The scoring formula:

(Productivity x 0.3) + (Learning x 0.25) + (Career x 0.25) + (Enjoyment x 0.2)

High scorers rise. Low scorers wait.

Example: 'Personal OS'

Score: 8.5
- Productivity: 9 (saves hours weekly)
- Learning: 8 (new architecture patterns)
- Career: 8 (great portfolio piece)
- Enjoyment: 9 (I actually want this)

Example: 'Random Twitter bot'

Score: 4.2
- Productivity: 2 (doesn't help my work)
- Learning: 5 (some API stuff)
- Career: 3 (not impressive)
- Enjoyment: 6 (kinda fun)

This one waits.

How to implement:

1. Create a simple form (Airtable, Google Sheets, or Telegram bot)
2. For each new idea, rate it 1-10 on your chosen dimensions
3. Calculate weighted score
4. Sort by score
5. Work on highest scorers first

Takeaway: Constraints increase creativity.

Knowing I'll only build high-scoring ideas makes me generate better ideas.

Quality thinking, not just quantity.

I need to verify THAT it works.

2. Implementation - Claude writes the code
3. Testing - I verify the behavior matches my specification
4. Iteration - If it doesn't work, we fix it together

- What the system should do
- What inputs it takes
- What outputs it produces
- What edge cases matter

What I DON'T try to understand:
- Specific syntax choices
- Library implementations
- Optimization details

The analogy:

I drive a car without understanding combustion engines.
I use a smartphone without understanding chip architecture.
I build software without understanding every function.

The caveat:

This works for personal tools and MVPs.

Production systems at scale? Different conversation. Know your context.

Takeaway: For most use cases, verification > comprehension. Test outputs, not code. Ship faster.

posts.title: How I manage 26 development projects without port conflicts
posts.body:
Every developer knows this pain:

Start a project. Port 3000 already in use.

Where's it running? Which project? Do I need it?

I built a system to eliminate this forever.

The Port Registry System:

A simple JSON file that tracks:
- Which project uses which port
- What type of service it is
- When it was last active

Port Allocation Strategy:

Web Apps (React, Vue): 3000-3099
Node/Express APIs: 4000-4099
Python (Flask/Django): 5000-5099
Go Applications: 6000-6099
Database Services: 7000-7099
Dev Tools: 9000-9099

The Workflow:

1. Before starting any service, check the registry
2. New project? Assign next available port in range
3. Update CLAUDE.md with port assignment
4. Claude always knows which port to use

How to implement:

1. Create a JSON file: ~/.port_registry.json
2. Structure: {project_name: {port: 3001, type: 'web', last_active: '2026-01-29'}}
3. Before starting a project, check the file
4. Update it when you start/stop services

Simple commands:

# Check what's running
lsof -i -P | grep LISTEN

# View your registry
cat ~/.port_registry.json

Results:
- Zero port conflicts in 6 months
- Instant context on any project
- Easy debugging when something's wrong

Takeaway: Small systems investments compound. 30 minutes setting up the registry saved hours of frustration.

posts.title: 5 prompting mistakes I made (and fixed) with Claude Code
tweets:
5 prompting mistakes I made (and fixed) with Claude Code.

Each one cost me hours of frustration.

Save yourself the pain:

Mistake #1: Asking for 'apps'

Bad: 'Build me an app that does X'

Problem: Too vague. Claude doesn't know scope, stack, or specifics.

Fix: Describe exact workflow. 'I need to upload a CSV, apply these rules, and download the result.'

Mistake #2: Dictating implementation

Bad: 'Use Python with BeautifulSoup and pandas to...'

Problem: I was guessing at the best approach.

Fix: Describe WHAT you need. 'I need to extract contact info from business websites.' Let Claude choose HOW.

Mistake #3: Giant prompts

Bad: 500-word specifications in one message.

Problem: Too much at once. Things get lost.

Fix: Break into steps. First the architecture. Then each component. One thing at a time.

Mistake #4: Ignoring context files

Bad: Re-explaining my project every session.

Problem: Massive waste of time. Inconsistent context.

Fix: Create CLAUDE.md with project overview, tech stack, current status. Claude reads it automatically.

Mistake #5: Hiding errors

Bad: Paraphrasing error messages.

Problem: Lost crucial debugging info.

Fix: Copy the EXACT error. Full stack trace. Let Claude see everything.

Bonus mistake: Expecting perfection

Bad: 'This should work the first time.'

Problem: Nothing works first time. That's normal.

Fix: Budget for 3-5 iterations. Errors are part of the process.

What changed after fixing these:

- Projects that took days now take hours
- Less frustration, more shipping
- Claude feels like a collaborator, not a slot machine

Takeaway: Prompting is a skill. You get better with practice.

The mistakes are part of learning.

Specific > vague. Small steps > big leaps. Exact errors > paraphrased problems.

posts.title: The gatekeeping around 'real programming' is getting embarrassing.
tweets:
The gatekeeping around 'real programming' is getting embarrassing.

'You didn't write it, AI did.'
'That's not real coding.'
'You don't understand what it does.'

Let's unpack this:

The core argument:

'If you didn't write the code line by line, you're not a real programmer.'

Okay. Let's follow that logic.

By that standard:

- Using libraries isn't real programming (you didn't write that code)
- Using frameworks isn't real programming
- Using StackOverflow isn't real programming
- Using autocomplete isn't real programming

Where's the line?

Programming has ALWAYS been about abstraction.

Assembly -> C -> Python -> AI

Each layer lets you focus on higher-level problems.

AI is just the next abstraction layer.

The actual skill being tested:

Can you solve problems?

Not: Can you type syntax?

What I can do:

- Define clear requirements
- Break complex problems into steps
- Test whether solutions work
- Debug when they don't
- Iterate to improvement

These are programming skills.

What I can't do:

- Write Python from memory
- Explain every function
- Pass a LeetCode interview

These used to be programming skills. They're becoming less relevant.

My output: 26 tools. Working. Useful. Some could be commercial.

Built by someone who can't write a for-loop from memory.

Takeaway: The gatekeeping misses the point.

The goal was never to write code.

The goal was to build things.

AI just changed HOW we build.

posts.title: The data cleanup workflow that handles any messy dataset
posts.body:
Every interesting dataset is messy.

Inconsistent formatting. Missing values. Duplicates. Garbage columns.

I've developed a repeatable workflow for cleaning any data.

Phase 1: Assessment (30 minutes)

- Sample 100 random rows
- Document every inconsistency found
- Identify patterns in the mess
- Estimate scope of cleanup needed

Phase 2: Rules Definition (1 hour)

- Write explicit transformation rules
- Define what 'clean' looks like for each field
- Document edge cases
- Create validation criteria

Phase 3: Implementation (varies)

The actual cleanup. But now with clear rules.

- Column mapping and standardization
- Pattern-based transformations
- Duplicate detection and handling
- Selective reprocessing for edge cases

Phase 4: Validation (30 minutes)

- Sample cleaned output
- Check against original requirements
- Verify edge cases handled
- Document any remaining issues

Key Features I Always Include:

1. State persistence - Resume from any point
2. Audit trail - Track every transformation
3. Selective reprocessing - Fix specific rows without rerunning everything
4. Version tracking - Roll back if needed

How to implement:

1. Start with a simple Python script
2. Add checkpointing (save progress every 1000 rows)
3. Log every transformation applied
4. Build a 'reprocess' function for specific rows

Takeaway: Most data problems are definition problems. Once you define exactly what you want, the implementation is straightforward.

posts.title: From raw IRS data to executive insights in one afternoon
posts.body:
A client asked for financial analysis of their nonprofit.

6 years of Form 990 filings.

The traditional approach: Weeks in spreadsheets.

My approach: Claude Code pipeline.

The Input:

Raw 990 data with:
- Revenue breakdowns
- Expense categories
- Salary information
- Asset/liability changes

The Process:

1. Data Extraction
Pull key metrics from each year. Ask Claude: 'Extract total revenue, total expenses, contributions, salaries from this 990.'

2. Trend Analysis
Calculate year-over-year changes. 'Compare these metrics across all 6 years. Flag anything changing more than 10% year over year.'

3. Ratio Analysis
Expense ratios, revenue mix, salary burden. 'Calculate program expense ratio, admin expense ratio, fundraising efficiency.'

4. Red Flag Detection
Automatic flagging of concerning trends. 'Based on nonprofit financial best practices, what should I be worried about?'

5. Narrative Generation
Transform data into readable insights. 'Write an executive summary explaining these findings to a board.'

The Discovery:

The organization went from profitable to $713K loss in two years.

Root causes:
- Expenses grew 15.8% while revenue grew 8.2%
- Contributions collapsed 69.8%
- Salary costs up 35.9% over 6 years

The Deliverable:
- Executive summary with key metrics
- Trend visualizations
- Root cause analysis
- Specific recommendations
- 3-year projection scenarios

Total Time: 4 hours

Takeaway: AI didn't do the analysis. I defined what questions to ask, validated the logic, interpreted findings, and crafted recommendations. AI handled data processing. Human + AI = faster, deeper analysis.
